name: Vertical Block Exemption Regulation
impact_assessment: Impact assessment report, May 2022 (SWD number not confirmed); evaluation SWD(2020) 172
evidence_rating: thin: no evaluation of the 2022 rules yet; causal evidence exists only for related national bans on hotel price-parity clauses
summary: The 2022 rules define which supply and distribution agreements are automatically allowed under EU competition law, with changes for online sales and platform price-parity clauses. No study has yet measured their effect. Earlier research on national bans of hotel-booking parity clauses found more price competition and some short-run price falls, which helped motivate the change.

indicators.objective: Commission regulation adopted under Article 101(3) TFEU - no legislative proposal or LFS indicators. The accompanying 2022 impact assessment and the 2020 evaluation of the 2010 VBER set the objectives; the Regulation expires 31 May 2034 and no ex-post evaluation exists yet
Legal certainty and lower compliance costs
indicators.indicator: Clearer safe harbour, reduced self-assessment costs for businesses
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The 2020 evaluation itself found too little quantitative data to assess compliance costs robustly.

indicators.objective: Adapt rules to online sales and platforms
indicators.indicator: Treatment of wide retail parity clauses (no longer block-exempted), online sales restrictions, dual distribution
indicators.evidence: No study of the 2022 rules' effects found. Earlier causal studies of national bans on hotel-booking parity clauses (Germany, France) found more room availability and direct-channel price competition and some short-run price falls - background evidence for the change.
indicators.sources: Hunold et al. 2018; Mantovani et al. 2021

indicators.objective: Prevent consumer harm from vertical restraints
indicators.indicator: Fewer harmful restrictions (e.g. resale price maintenance, territorial restrictions)
indicators.evidence: Enforcement continues case by case; no aggregate measure.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Evaluation of the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation and Vertical Guidelines (Staff Working Document), SWD(2020) 172
literature.title: Evaluation of the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation and Vertical Guidelines (Staff Working Document)
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (external study, public consultation, case studies)
literature.outcomes: legal certainty; compliance costs; online sales
literature.headline: 2010 VBER useful and still relevant but not adapted to growth of online sales and platforms; some definitions unclear; diverging national interpretation; costs could not be quantified robustly due to lack of data
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's review of the 2010 rules found them still useful but outdated for e-commerce and online platforms, and could not put numbers on their costs or benefits.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact assessment report accompanying the revised Vertical Block Exemption Regulation and Vertical Guidelines, Commission staff working document (May 2022)
literature.title: Impact assessment report accompanying the revised Vertical Block Exemption Regulation and Vertical Guidelines
literature.outcomes: legal certainty; online sales; parity clauses; dual distribution
literature.headline: Published with the revised rules (VBER adopted 10 May 2022, in force 1 June 2022; Guidelines 30 June 2022); SWD reference not confirmed
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's assessment underpinned changes to how the competition rules treat online sales, platforms and price-parity clauses.

literature.citation: Hunold, Kesler, Laitenberger & Schlutter (2018), Evaluation of best price clauses in online hotel bookings, International Journal of Industrial Organization 61: 542-571
literature.title: Evaluation of best price clauses in online hotel bookings
literature.method: difference-in-differences (meta-search price data, ~30,000 hotels, several countries)
literature.headline: After Booking.com's narrow parity clause was abolished in Germany, hotels offered rooms more often on Booking.com and more often promoted their direct channel; chain hotels' direct channel more often had the strictly lowest price
literature.summary_plain: A study of nearly 30,000 hotels found that when price-parity clauses were removed, hotels listed more rooms and more often undercut booking platforms on their own websites.
literature.period_geography: Germany and other European countries, mid-2010s

literature.citation: Mantovani, Piga & Reggiani (2021), Online platform price parity clauses: Evidence from the EU Booking.com case, European Economic Review 131: 103625
literature.title: Online platform price parity clauses: Evidence from the EU Booking.com case
literature.method: difference-in-differences (posted Booking.com prices, France vs controls)
literature.headline: Removal of price parity clauses in France in 2015 led to significant price decreases in the short run but a more limited effect in the medium run; hotels with more complex structures cut prices more
literature.summary_plain: Hotel prices on Booking.com fell after France banned price-parity clauses, though the effect faded over time.
